content: Twin pregnancies are associated with a higher risk of perinatal mortality, primarily due to prematurity. However, complications during labor and delivery can also contribute to perinatal loss or morbidity. To mitigate these risks, the option of a planned caesarean section should be considered. Nevertheless, evidence from randomized trials of other obstetric interventions, such as planned caesarean section for breech presentation and continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring, has revealed unexpected discrepancies between short-term perinatal morbidity and long-term neurological outcomes. Additionally, the risks of caesarean section for the mother, both in the current pregnancy and in future pregnancies, must be carefully evaluated. The objective of this review was to assess the shortand long-term effects of planned caesarean section for twin pregnancies on both mothers and their babies. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched, along with reference lists of relevant studies, up to November 18, 2015. Randomized trials comparing planned caesarean section with planned vaginal birth for women with twin pregnancies were included. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the studies and extracted data. The quality of evidence for key outcomes was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Two trials were included in the review. The majority of the data came from a large multicenter trial involving 2804 women across 106 centers in 25 countries. These centers were equipped to perform emergency caesarean sections and had the necessary anesthetic, obstetric, and nursing staff available during planned vaginal deliveries. The second trial, conducted in Israel, included 60 women. The risk of bias was judged to be low for most categories, except for performance bias (high) and outcome assessment bias (unclear). There was no clear evidence of differences in maternal death or serious maternal morbidity between women randomized to planned caesarean section versus planned vaginal birth (risk ratio [RR] 0.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.11; 2844 women; two studies; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference between the groups in terms of perinatal or neonatal death or serious neonatal morbidity (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.67; data for 5565 babies; one study; moderate-quality evidence). None of the studies reported on childhood disability. For secondary outcomes, there was no clear evidence of differences between the groups in perinatal or neonatal mortality (RR 1.41, 95% CI 0.76 to 2.62; 5685 babies; two studies; moderate-quality evidence) or serious neonatal morbidity (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.64; 5644 babies; two studies; moderate-quality evidence). Other neonatal outcomes also showed no significant differences between the groups. The number of women undergoing caesarean section was reported in both trials. In the planned caesarean section group, 90.9% of women underwent the procedure as planned. In contrast, 42.9% of women in the planned vaginal birth group required a caesarean section for at least one twin. Maternal mortality was rare, with no events reported in one trial and two deaths (one in each group) in the other. There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of serious maternal morbidity overall (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.11; 2844 women; two studies) or specific types of short-term maternal morbidity. There were also no significant differences between the groups in terms of breastfeeding failure (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.38; 2570 women; one study; moderate-quality evidence) or the number of women scoring above 12 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.14; 2570 women; one study; moderate-quality evidence). The authors concluded that data, primarily from one large multicenter study, did not provide clear evidence of benefit from planned caesarean section for term twin pregnancies with a leading cephalic presentation. Long-term infant outcomes remain unknown. Women should be informed about the potential risks and benefits of labor and vaginal birth based on their specific clinical circumstances, as well as the shortand long-term implications of caesarean section for both themselves and their babies. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine planned caesarean section for term twin pregnancies with a leading cephalic presentation, except within the context of further randomized trials.
